claims.text: The as-cast nominally equiatomic WTaVTi precursor has W/Ta-rich dendrites and Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels.
Liquid-metal dealloying in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 hours selectively extracts Ti from the interdendritic regions.
The dealloying treatment creates a directionally aligned bicontinuous RHEA–Cu composite.
The resulting structure contains approximately 64 vol.% BCC RHEA ligaments and 36 vol.% nearly pure FCC Cu channels.
An approximately 300 nm thick W-rich interlayer forms spontaneously at each RHEA/Cu interface.
The processed composite contains minor HCP Ti-rich precipitates.
A negative heat of mixing between Ti and Cu drives preferential Ti dissolution from the precursor.
Preferential Ti dissolution leaves a W–Ta–V framework that forms the RHEA ligaments.
A strong positive heat of mixing between W and Cu traps W at RHEA/Cu interfaces.
The interfacial W-rich layer passivates the interfaces and stabilizes the bicontinuous architecture.
Directionally aligned Cu channels enhance heat conduction through the composite.
The complex RHEA lattice resists helium-induced defect migration.
Resistance to helium-induced defect migration curtails irradiation-induced swelling.
Above approximately 650 °C, the processed composite will have substantially higher thermal conductivity than the unprocessed WTaVTi precursor.
At high temperature, the processed composite will have higher thermal conductivity than pure W.
The composite's thermal-conductivity advantage will peak above 1000 °C.
Under 25 keV He+ irradiation, the processed composite will exhibit less swelling than pure W.
Under 25 keV He+ irradiation, blistering in the processed composite will begin later than in pure W.
The expected benefits are confined to directionally segregated WTaVTi precursors processed by liquid-metal dealloying at 1200 °C for 96 hours.
The predicted irradiation benefit has not been established for neutron irradiation or other higher-energy irradiation environments.
